questions.q: Define anchorage dependence and name one cell type that exhibits it and one that does not.
questions.a: Anchorage dependence is the requirement for cells to adhere to a solid substrate via ECM-integrin interactions to proliferate. Fibroblasts and epithelial cells are anchorage-dependent; hematopoietic stem cells and many tumor-derived lines (e.g., HeLa, suspension-adapted CHO) are anchorage-independent. A wrong answer (e.g., "all animal cells are anchorage-dependent") reveals confusion between primary cells and continuous lines, or ignorance of blood-derived cells.

questions.q: A student observes that a primary fibroblast culture stops growing when the flask bottom is fully covered, but a HeLa culture continues to pile up into multilayers. Explain this difference using the concept of contact inhibition.
questions.a: Normal fibroblasts exhibit contact inhibition: cell-cell contact (via cadherins) activates the Hippo pathway, leading to YAP/TAZ cytoplasmic retention and p27^Kip1^-mediated G1 arrest at confluence. HeLa cells have lost contact inhibition due to transformation (e.g., HPV E6/E7 inactivating p53/Rb), so they ignore density signals and overgrow. A wrong answer citing "nutrient depletion" or "space limitation" misses the active signaling mechanism and the defining feature of transformation.

questions.q: You are given a new cell line "X". Design a simple two-step experiment to test whether it is anchorage-dependent and whether it shows contact inhibition.
questions.a: Step 1 (anchorage): Seed cells in parallel on (a) tissue-culture treated plastic (adhesive) and (b) ultra-low attachment plates or poly-HEMA coated plates (non-adhesive). After 48h, assess viability/proliferation (e.g., MTT). Anchorage-dependent cells die/arrest on non-adhesive surface; independent cells grow. Step 2 (contact inhibition): Seed cells at low density on adhesive surface, let them reach confluence, and continue culture 3-4 more days. Monitor by phase-contrast: contact-inhibited cells remain a flat monolayer; non-inhibited cells pile up/focus. A wrong design (e.g., only testing one condition) fails to isolate the variables.

questions.q: Compare the roles of serum and the culture vessel surface in supporting anchorage-dependent growth. Why is serum alone insufficient for attachment on a non-treated plastic dish?
questions.a: Serum provides adhesion factors (fibronectin, vitronectin) that adsorb onto the charged/hydrophilic surface of tissue-culture treated plastic, creating an ECM-like coating for integrin binding. Non-treated plastic is hydrophobic; serum proteins denature/adsorb poorly, failing to present functional RGD motifs. Thus, both a treated surface (to anchor proteins in correct conformation) and serum (to supply the proteins) are needed. A wrong answer saying "serum contains nutrients so cells grow anywhere" ignores the structural role of adsorbed ECM.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Loss of contact inhibition is sufficient to make a finite cell line continuous (immortal)."
questions.a: False. Loss of contact inhibition allows overgrowth at high density, but immortality requires additional events: bypassing senescence (e.g., telomerase activation, p53/pRb pathway inactivation) and often anchorage independence. Many transformed lines are contact-inhibited but immortal (e.g., some viral-transformed lines), while others lose contact inhibition but still senesce. A student saying "true" conflates transformation phenotypes; the Hayflick limit (senescence) is distinct from density-dependent arrest.

questions.q: Create a hypothetical scenario where a researcher wants to produce a recombinant protein from an anchorage-dependent cell line at 10,000 L scale. Propose a strategy that addresses both anchorage dependence and contact inhibition limitations.
questions.a: Use microcarrier beads (e.g., Cytodex) in a stirred-tank bioreactor: beads provide high surface-area-to-volume for attachment (solving anchorage), and cells grow as monolayers on beads until contact inhibition halts proliferation. To extend production, use a perfusion system to remove waste/add nutrients while retaining cells/beads, or engineer the line to express a temperature-sensitive SV40 T-antigen to conditionally bypass contact inhibition at production phase. A poor answer suggests "just use a bigger flask" (ignores scale) or "switch to suspension culture" (ignores anchorage dependence of the line).

What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Anchorage dependence?
questions.a: Students often think "contact inhibition" means cells physically cannot divide because there is no space — a passive crowding effect.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can (1) distinguish anchorage-dependent vs anchorage-independent cells with examples, (2) explain the molecular basis of contact inhibition (density-dependent inhibition of growth), and (3) predict culture behavior (monolayer formation, need for passaging, loss of contact inhibition in cancer cells) for a given cell type.
